OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define risk management and its relevance in the field of orthopaedic surgery.
Identify specific risks for patients and providers inside and outside the operating room.
Discuss risk management processes.
Review risk management processes in unique situations.
Background
Risk management is a broad and industry-traversing term used to describe measures to mitigate, minimize, and/or
eliminate negative outcomes or failure.

Background
The definition and use of risk management vary based on the context. For example, in the business world, risk
management often is defined as measures taken by a company or organization to identify and minimize
actions that may lead to reduced success.1 Risk management may include complex tools for risk identification
and analysis with the ultimate goal of risk reduction.2 Effective risk management strategies should deliver safe
and effective products or services to consumers, with minimal risk of failure.3

In health care, risk management may refer to patient-, hospital-, provider-, or business-level risks. In medicine,
the primary goal of any risk management system is to mitigate or eliminate negative outcomes or failures. For
example, a hospital system may use specific disaster risk management structures that include risk assessment,
pre-disaster planning, prevention and mitigation, preparedness, response tactics, and recovery.4 As it relates to
patient care, risk management should reduce or eliminate adverse events. In addition to the effect of medical
errors on patients, medical errors cost more than $9 billion annually in the United States alone.5
Medical Errors
Medical errors, or adverse events, may contribute to as many as 98,000 deaths per year in the United States.6
Medical errors include wrong-site surgery, falls, postoperative complications, and other poor patient outcomes.
Medical errors may lead to ligation.

Medical Errors
Adverse events refer to the broad spectrum of health care failures and include wrong-site surgery, erroneous
diagnoses, falls, infection, postoperative complications, and incorrect therapies.7 Medical errors often lead to
frustrated providers, patient dissatisfaction, and even poorer patient outcomes. If errors occur, the surgeon
and provider team must remain professional and compassionate. Avoiding unnecessary and inappropriate
confrontation is important to continuing to provide safe and effective patient care in the setting of medical
errors. Hasty hospital discharge and anger-driven unproductive communication must be avoided.
Ultimately, medical errors may lead to litigation. Malpractice claims may involve orthopaedic surgery in as
many as 20% to 36% of cases.8,9 Often, incompetence, neglect, work overload, and/or staff shortages
contribute to these adverse events.10 Litigation in orthopaedic surgery frequently is related to wrong-site
surgery, which accounts for 2% of medical malpractice claims against orthopaedic surgeons; in most of these
cases (>80%), courts have sided with the plaintiff.11,12
Unfortunately, adverse events are common in medicine. In orthopaedic surgery specifically, as many as 65% of
providers reported mistakes in the clinical work environment each week.13 The focus of this lesson is risk
management, highlighting strategies used to mitigate adverse events for patients and providers within the field
of orthopaedic surgery. Risk management strategies in the inpatient and outpatient setting and improvement
methods are outlined. A thorough understanding of risk management is critical to providing successful, high-
quality orthopaedic surgical care.
Risk Management
Overview


Overview
Defining the spectrum of risks and adverse events that exist for patients and their prevalence is the first step to
understanding patient risk. An understanding of the phase of the care process in which orthopaedic medicine
adverse events occur better enables surgeons to effectively mitigate such risks via several strategies. For
example, adverse events or failures may occur during the perioperative period, intraoperative period, in the
inpatient environment, or in the outpatient setting.
Preoperative Risk and Management
Adverse events may occur during the preoperative period in outpatient and inpatient settings.
Elective, urgent, and emergent surgeries are subject to failure and adverse events.
Preoperative checklists may improve perioperative safety.
Operating room sign-in, time-out, and sign-out should always be performed.
Surgical site marking helps reduce the risk of wrong-site surgery.
A team approach is critical in the prevention of preoperative adverse events.

Preoperative Risk and Management
Adverse events, such as wound dehiscence, infection, and venous thromboembolism (VTE) more frequently
occur with emergent surgery.14,15 The preoperative period includes the period from the time the patient
arrives for surgical treatment to the time surgical treatment occurs. Various steps that must occur before the
patient is in the operating room. Hospital and nursing staff often facilitate the check-in process for patients,
establish intravenous access, verify nothing-by-mouth status, verify patient identification, discuss planned
procedures, document surgical consent completion, and confirm an updated patient history and physical
examination have occurred and have been documented by the orthopaedic care team. Breakdown of any of
these steps may result in failure or poor outcomes of the planned surgical procedure (ie, adverse events). In
the business world, various benchmark metrics, checkpoints, and checklists may be used to evaluate and
maintain the consistent positive performance of business operations—a system commonly referred to as
process metrics. The use of checklists during the preoperative stages of care progression in orthopaedic
surgery promotes patient safety.16
In conjunction with the World Health Organization and the Joint Commission Universal Protocol, the
Association for periOperative Registered Nurses developed a comprehensive checklist to be used during the
perioperative setting.17 The checklist includes the standard operating room sign-in, time-out, and sign-out;
however, the preprocedural check-in occurs in the preoperative holding area and is primarily a preoperative
nursing-driven risk management strategy. The following are key principles in the preoperative checklist:17
Patient identification

Procedure and procedure site marking
Consent
Patient history and physical examination
Pre-anesthesia and nursing assessment
Diagnostic and radiologic test results
Blood products
Special equipment, devices, implants
Prophylaxis plan for VTE
Beta-blocker medication administration if indicated
Between 30% and 50% of spine surgeons and more than 20% of hand surgeons surveyed reported operating
on the wrong site during their career.18-20 A critical component of all preoperative risk management strategies
must be surgical site marking. This allows for quick and simple confirmation of the correct extremity and/or the
planned surgical site by all members of the surgical team. In 1997, the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons instituted the Sign Your Site campaign to encourage orthopaedic surgeon compliance with surgical
site marking.21,22
Evidence suggests that as many as 16% of surgeons planned to operate on the wrong site before noticing their
error during the site-marking process.21 This is a key risk management strategy that ideally is performed by the
attending orthopaedic surgeon; however, institutional variation exists. Although site marking typically is
performed by an individual, preventing wrong-site surgery is the responsibility of the entire preoperative and
surgical team. Therefore, at each care handoff before the planned surgical procedure, surgical site marking
must be verified. The correct side of surgery also must be verified because communication breakdown
regarding which side (left versus right) may occur.
Intraoperative Risk and Management
Intraoperative risk that may lead to poor patient outcomes and other failures include the following: wrong-site
surgery, sterile field contamination, needlesticks, and patient decompensation.
Standardized checklists are critical in minimizing intraoperative risk. 
All components of a sign-in, time-out, and sign-out must be completed to identify areas of concern by all team
members.

Intraoperative Risk and Management
A standardized checklist that includes sign-in, time-out, and sign-out also is critical for intraoperative risk
management and mitigation strategies. Such a checklist was developed by the Association for periOperative
Registered Nurses in conjunction with the World Health Organization and the Joint Commission.17,23
Meticulous use of this intraoperative checklist is the single most effective risk management strategy to
decrease adverse events.24 Consistent checklist use reduces intraoperative complication rates and mortality.25-

28 Three common phases of intraoperative checklists include sign-in, time-out, and sign-out. These steps
should be completed during every case and all operating room activities should be suspended during this
discussion, except in the case of life-threatening emergencies.
The surgical sign-in is completed before the induction of anesthesia and frequently is performed by the
anesthesia staff in combination with the operating room nurse and surgical team. At the end of the sign-in
checklist, all operating room team members address concerns openly and review the care plan. The following
aspects typically are included during the sign-in:17
Confirmation of patient identification, procedure, and site
Consent cross-reference and confirmation
Site marking
Patient allergies discussed
Blood loss risk and airway risk
Vital sign monitoring by anesthesia confirmed
Institution anesthesia checklist complete
The surgical time-out checklist is completed by the primary surgeon and is performed before skin incision. This
phase should include the following:17
Repeat confirmation of patient identification, procedure, and site
Consent cross-reference and confirmation
Site marking
Fire risk prevention discussion
Imaging studies displayed
Equipment availability and concerns
Anticipated case duration and blood loss
Antibiotic prophylaxis administered before skin incision
Finally, the surgical sign-out checklist is completed before the patient leaves the operating room. The sign-out
is critical to risk management in the operating room and prevention of adverse events and often is an
important time for plan communication among operating room team members before the postanesthesia care
unit handoff. This phase is subject to the highest incidence of medical errors compared with the other
phases.29 A thorough and complete surgical sign-out includes the following:17
Procedure performed
Completion and accuracy of sharp, sponge, and instrument counts
Specimens sent
Wound classification
Prevention of VTE
Discussion of weight-bearing status and postoperative plan
Debriefing of operating room care team

Inpatient Risk and Management
Inpatient risks to patients include falls, infections, VTE, deep vein thrombosis, wound complications, and unplanned
return to the operating room.
Falls occur at a rate of 0.5% to 2.0% and may result in injury in 30% of patients.
Effective communication among staff is important to decrease fall risk.
Workarounds that decrease work load may lead to an increase in poor communication and the perpetuation of
misinformation.
Several protocols exist to improve communication, such as SBAR (situation, background, assessment,
recommendation) tool.

Inpatient Risk and Management
The inpatient setting encompasses patient care during planned or unplanned admission for orthopaedic
treatment and patient care in the postoperative phase after discharge from the postanesthesia care unit.
Risk management strategies are used to successfully reduce the risks for adverse events outside of the
operating room. Although adverse respiratory events are the leading cause of mortality in the perioperative
period, it the risks for other adverse events must be considered.30 Examples of inpatient and postoperative
risks include adverse events related to patient falls, infection, VTE, wound complications, and unplanned return
to the operating room. Several inpatient risk management strategies may be used to aid in risk reduction.
In-hospital falls are a relatively common but devastating adverse event after orthopaedic surgery. Falls occur
0.5% to 2% of the time after major joint replacement procedures, with as many as 30% of falls resulting in
patient injury.31,32 Falls during inpatient rehabilitation occur at rates as high as 9.5% and are more likely to
occur during daylight hours and be unwitnessed.33 Systems-based approaches targeting high-risk situations
have successfully prevented falls resulting in injuries on orthopaedic wards.34 A systematic and standardized
quality improvement approach, including problem definition, cause identification, action plan and outcome
metric development, implementation, and outcome analysis, was used to implement a successful fall-
prevention intervention focusing on safe toileting and shoulder-support safety as a risk management
strategy.34 An effective risk management strategy for fall prevention also must address fall prevention after the
patient has been cleared for hospital discharge because falls frequently occur in the first and second year
postoperatively.35
Another critical risk management tool to mitigate adverse events in the inpatient setting involves effective
communication. Communication errors are a risk factor for adverse events in orthopaedics.13,36 Almost 25% of
the time, communication is a major contributing factor leading to adverse events in orthopaedics.37 Effective
communication is critical at every phase of care, from clinical evaluation to hospital discharge after orthopaedic
surgery. The balance of effective and efficient communication often is difficult. Effective and thorough

communication may not always be efficient. Several workarounds for this may exist; one workaround
commonly used is the copy forward function in many electronic medical records (EMRs), which allows for easy
note templates and structures to be copied forward for editing and updating. Unfortunately, copied notes may
perpetuate misleading and inaccurate information and may lead to serious communication errors.38
Protocols for successful communication exist. For example, simple but standardized memory cues have been
used in German hospitals and may improve care team recall of important patient data during handoffs.39 The I-
PASS (illness severity, patient summary, action list, situation awareness, synthesis by receiver) method is an
evidence-based and standardized method for patient handoffs that has been shown to decrease medical
errors by 23% to 40%.40,41 Another simple handoff method commonly employed is the SBAR tool.42-46 Having
an easy and reproducible framework for clear and concise communication at each stage of an orthopaedic
patient’s care team change is critical to mitigating the risk of adverse events. Communication and/or handoff
errors are the key cause of as many as two-thirds of medical sentinel events.41 Other toolkits are available to
aid in risk reduction in the inpatient setting.
Finally, orthopaedic surgery patients frequently are subject to weight-bearing restrictions, immobilization, and
tissue damage from injury or surgery—all of which are major factors for increased VTE risk. For example, the
combined incidence of VTE among patients who undergo below-the-knee orthopaedic surgery is approximately
2.5%.47,48 Although a thorough discussion of VTE prophylaxis protocols in each subspecialty is beyond the
scope of this lesson and is variable and institution-dependent, several key overarching risk management
strategies may be used to prevent VTE. First, orthopaedic surgeons must be aware of and practice in the
confines of specialty-specific and academy recommendations related to VTE prophylaxis. In addition, a
thorough and complete clinical history is critical in ascertaining a patient’s history of VTE and/or risk factors for
VTE, such as protein C or S deficiency. These risk factors and practice management strategies are important
components in mitigating VTE risk for all practicing orthopaedic surgeons regardless of specialty-specific
recommendations and particular VTE prophylaxis practices.
Outpatient Risk and Management
Medical errors in the outpatient setting often include lower acuity problems.
Several steps must occur in the outpatient setting before patients can be safely taken to the operating room or the
inpatient setting.
Ideally, the surgical consent process should occur in the outpatient setting.
A discrepancy often exists between a surgeon’s perception and a patient’s perception of surgical consent.
Effective and empathetic communication in orthopaedic surgery practice may decrease litigation claims against
orthopaedic surgeons.
The outpatient setting in orthopaedics includes various office encounters and nonsurgical orthopaedic management
practices. These encounters broadly include the following:
Clinic visits for new patient evaluations
Follow-up management of nonsurgical treatment
Postoperative management

Preoperative counseling

Outpatient Risk and Management
Although the nonsurgical setting may represent a lower level of inherent risk for adverse patient outcomes and
medical errors given the lower acuity of in-office orthopaedic problems and management strategies, several
important parameters must be appropriately addressed in the outpatient setting. Several steps in the
preoperative visit and in the routine clinical care of many orthopaedic pathologies put the patient at risk for
adverse events, errors in diagnosis, unexpected treatment failures, or communication errors. The following
represent critical steps in outpatient orthopaedic surgery clinical practice and are risk factors for adverse
events if their processes are poorly executed:49
Surgical consent process
Effective communication and EMR management
Each year, more than 200 million patients worldwide are exposed to the risks of surgical procedures.50 The
surgical consent process is a critical step in the practice of orthopaedic surgery and should serve as a risk-
reduction tool; however, orthopaedic surgeons consistently are not viewed as effective and empathetic
communicators in the medical community and among patients.51 Patients’ perception of their perceived
involvement in medical decision making has been shown to be consistently lower than observed involvement
by research study teams.52 In addition, a disconnect exists with regard to how well orthopaedic surgeons think
they communicate versus how patients perceive the strength of communication. One group demonstrated that
75% of orthopaedic surgeons believed they communicated effectively, whereas only 21% of patients believed
effective communication took place.53
Having tools for an effective consent discussion and good surgeon-patient communication may help mitigate
treatment risks in the perioperative setting. Ensuring that patients understand the planned surgical procedure,
alternative treatment options, risks, advantages, and common complications is the first step toward mitigating
failures, such as postoperative complications. Establishing realistic treatment expectations with patients also
should be part of all consent processes; however, lack of uniformity exists in the orthopaedic surgical consent
process, and information presentation is variable.54,55
Orthopaedic surgery is one of the top five subspecialties most at risk for litigation.56 Numerous errors in the
consent process contribute to litigation against orthopaedic surgeons.57 Risk of litigation must not be the
driving factor for obtaining appropriate and thorough consent; however, failure to do so puts the surgeon and
patient at risk. Lawsuits involving malpractice claims suggest that documentation of an appropriate informed
consent process in office notes is associated with a decreased risk of indemnity payout after elective surgery;58
however, obtaining consent in the hospital has been associated with increased indemnity payout risk.58
Therefore, surgical consent for elective procedures should occur in the office setting if possible.

The informed consent process requires that a physician obtain consent before any treatment is rendered or
surgical procedure is performed and before many diagnostic procedures are performed. Without informed
consent, the physician may be held liable for violation of a patient’s rights, regardless whether the treatment
was appropriate and rendered with due care. Medical care cannot be provided without expressed or implied
permission for the physician to act.
The optimal consent process should include, at a minimum, a discussion of the following:57
Planned surgical procedure, including planned surgical site
Risks of planned surgical procedure
Advantages of planned surgical procedure
Expected outcomes of planned surgical procedure
Risk, advantages, and expected outcomes of alternative treatment options to planned surgical procedure
Relevant patient identification information (medical record number, name, date of birth)
Likely period of recovery and recovery expectations
Common and uncommon complications of surgical management
Effective communication in the busy outpatient setting is another critical risk management strategy. With the
advent, transition, and full incorporation of EMRs, medical information has become more accessible and more
abundant; however, EMRs are associated with numerous risks related to the management of imaging studies
and test results. For example, poor use of EMR features may result in inaccurate data in the EMR and
predispose patients to adverse events.59,60 In addition, although EMR use may result in improved
communication and follow-up of imaging studies and test results, providers across specialties often rely on
workarounds if limited EMR functionality affects efficient practice; this ultimately results in an increased risk of
adverse events.61-63 Mitigating the risks of an EMR is critical to decreasing adverse events. A timely review of
new or updated diagnostic and treatment data is imperative to the prevention of medical errors.49
In addition, appropriate use of a support staff team (office managers, nursing staff, advanced practice
providers) in the management of medical data may help mitigate inherent risks in data management and
information overload for orthopaedic surgeons. In addition, several other office support staff team members
are critical to preventing communication breakdown. For example, the use of trained and standardized
language interpretation services (rather than family members) is important for optimal and clear patient-
surgeon communication.
Effective and empathetic communication in orthopaedic surgery practice may decrease litigation claims against
orthopaedic surgeons. Numerous studies have demonstrated that if appropriate and compassionate
communication skills are employed, the risk of litigation is decreased.9,64-66 If litigation does ensue, patients
must prove a number of elements to be successful. These include the following:
Duty
Breach of duty

Causation
Damage
Duty is the physician’s obligation to care for a patient in a manner that is consistent with the quality of care
provided by other physicians in managing a patient’s condition. Breach of duty implies that the facts show that
the physician failed to meet the standard of care in treating the patient. In addition, a poor outcome,
regardless whether permanent, or a predictable complication does not necessarily mean that the physician has
deviated from the standard of care. Causation is proof that the violation caused the patient’s injury. Finally,
damage implies that proof exists that the physician’s deviation from the standard of care resulted in physical,
emotional, or financial injury to the patient.
Quality Improvement: Institutionalized Risk Management Strategies
Clear and efficient use of a systems approach for identifying and addressing medical errors via a quality
improvement process is vital.
The first step after a medical error occurs often includes a clear, open, and empathetic discussion with the patient
and/or his or her family.
Many hospitals have processes in place for the investigation and management of sentinel events or medical errors
and subsequent quality improvement.

Quality Improvement: Institutionalized Risk Management Strategies
Focused systems for medical error identification and analysis are critical to patient safety, quality, and
management of treatment failure risks and adverse events;67 however, risk management strategies are
valuable only if they reduce medical errors or improve the processes leading to medical errors. Several quality
improvement paradigms exist and are used to better understand medical errors and the reasons they occur. A
systems-based approach for identifying and understanding medical errors has been suggested.68
If adverse events occur, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guidelines suggest that errors should
be discussed “directly with a patient/family member in an honest, compassionate manner.”69 However, the
next steps often are not taken to ensure appropriate risk management strategies are put in place to decrease
future risk. Many hospitals have processes in place for the investigation and management of sentinel events or
medical errors and subsequent quality improvement. The Six Sigma technique is used in many settings.70 This
approach includes a number of standardized steps aimed at reducing variation and failures in processes71:
Define
Measure
Analyze
Improve
Control

During the define and measure phases, system processes and potential causes of a specific adverse event
often are identified via value stream mapping and Ishikawa fishbone diagrams, respectively.72 Data gathered
during these processes are then analyzed to understand the root causes of medical errors. Quality
improvement processes are then implemented and verified and are monitored for success. Finally, during the
control phase, practices are put into place to sustain gains achieved during the prior phases of the Six Sigma
technique. Other techniques distill the quality improvement process down to four phases: plan, do, study,
act.73,74
Regardless of the technique used for quality improvement and medical error monitoring and data analysis,
implementation of such a strategy for risk management is important for mitigating medical errors in
orthopaedic surgery. In addition, orthopaedic surgeons’ knowledge of and participation in an institution’s
quality improvement process is crucial to reduce medical errors and decrease adverse events in
orthopaedics.73,75
Mark as Complete
